passage: At outdoor time, five-year-old Payal lay on the school grass and shouted, "A dragon! Look, his tail!" The cloud stretched across the sky, and she roared at it, giggling. After lunch, the nap room was dim. Payal opened her eyes and froze. On the wall, the coat rack's shadow had long arms and a lumpy head. She pulled the sheet over her face and whimpered. Ms Vandana came and knelt. "What do you see?" "A monster." Ms Vandana switched on the small lamp. The monster became hooks and a raincoat. Payal peeked out. "It was a cloud shape," she whispered.

qa.q: What did the coat rack's shadow turn into when the lamp came on?
qa.a: Hooks and a raincoat.

qa.q: How did Payal feel at nap time, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Frightened 😰 She froze, pulled the sheet over her face and whimpered.

qa.q: What did Ms Vandana choose to do, and why did it help?
qa.a: She knelt, asked what Payal saw and switched on the small lamp, so Payal could see for herself that the monster was hooks and a raincoat.

qa.q: What would change if Ms Vandana had only said "There's no monster, go to sleep"?
qa.a: Payal might have stayed scared under the sheet, because she would not have seen the shadow change for herself.

grounding: A preschooler delights in a dragon cloud and later fears a shadow monster, both from seeing shapes.

passage: I'm Abhinav, and my neighbour Irfan, who's five, sleeps over sometimes. On Saturday evening we lay on the terrace, and Irfan pointed up. "An elephant! With a long nose!" He laughed so much he got hiccups. Later, in my room, the fan made a spinning shadow on the ceiling. Irfan grabbed my arm. "Spider. Big spider." He wouldn't let go. I don't know what he really saw. Maybe the same kind of shapes, just scarier in the dark. I switched the fan off and the shadow stopped. Irfan sighed and fell asleep holding my sleeve.

qa.q: What did Irfan see in the clouds?
qa.a: An elephant with a long nose.

qa.q: What does Irfan grabbing Abhinav's arm suggest?
qa.a: He was scared of the spinning shadow, which looked to him like a big spider.

qa.q: What did Abhinav do that helped Irfan settle?
qa.a: Switched the fan off so the shadow stopped moving, which took away the "spider" without any argument.

qa.q: Why can Abhinav only guess what Irfan saw?
qa.a: Abhinav watches from outside; only Irfan knows what shape he saw in the shadow, and a five-year-old may not be able to explain it.

grounding: A neighbour watches a young child laugh at an elephant cloud and then fear a spider shadow at night.

passage: Monday morning, on the walk to school, Disha tugged Mehak's hand. "Mumma, a rabbit cloud! Its ears are flopping!" She hopped like a rabbit all the way to the gate. Wednesday night, Disha screamed. The curtain's shadow on her wall had a pointy hat and bony fingers. Mehak held her until her breathing slowed. Friday night, Mehak brought a torch. "Let's make shadows." She made a dog; Disha made a wobbly bird. Then Disha pointed at the curtain. "That's just a curtain witch. She's friends with my bird." She giggled and switched the torch off.

qa.q: What did the curtain's shadow have?
qa.a: A pointy hat and bony fingers.

qa.q: How did Disha feel about the curtain shadow by Friday, and what shows it?
qa.a: Much less scared 🙂 She called it "just a curtain witch" who is friends with her bird, and giggled.

qa.q: Which choice by Mehak helped change Disha's fear?
qa.a: Bringing a torch on Friday to make shadow animals, so Disha could see that she could make shapes herself.

qa.q: What was Wednesday night like for Mehak?
qa.a: Mehak had to calm a screaming child and hold her until her breathing slowed, which may have been worrying and tiring.

grounding: Over one week, a young girl delights in a rabbit cloud, is frightened by a shadow, and then plays with shadows herself.

passage:
Before the storm, Hansa, five, pointed at the sky from the doorstep. "Arohi Didi! A dragon! See his fire?" A long grey cloud with a flaming orange edge. She roared and flapped her arms.
That night the power went out. Didi lit a candle. On the wall, the clothes on the hook swelled into a giant with a lumpy head. Hansa froze, then dived under the quilt.
"Hansa, look." Didi lifted the candle. The giant slid sideways and shrank. "It's only Papa's shirt."
Hansa peeped out. She made a bird with her fingers.

qa.q: What did Hansa see in the cloud before the storm?
qa.a: A dragon, with fire along its edge.

qa.q: Why did Hansa dive under the quilt?
qa.a: The shadow of the clothes looked like a giant to her, and she was frightened in the dark.

qa.q: What did Arohi Didi do that helped, and why did it work?
qa.a: She moved the candle so Hansa could see the giant shrink and was only Papa's shirt, turning fear back into play.

qa.q: How might Arohi Didi feel when Hansa makes a bird with her fingers?
qa.a: Didi would likely feel relieved and pleased that Hansa is playing again instead of hiding.

grounding: A child delights in a dragon cloud and fears a shadow giant, both from seeing shapes in patterns.

passage:
On the terrace of their Mumbai building, Lakshmi, five, lay on the water tank lid with Amma, Sangeeta. "A crocodile! Amma, his mouth is open!" She snapped her hands like jaws and laughed till she hiccupped.
At bedtime, car lights swept through the window. Stripes from the grill slid across the ceiling like long fingers. "Amma! A monster!" Lakshmi pressed her face into Sangeeta's arm.
Sangeeta held her. "Watch. Here comes the next car." The stripes swept again, and vanished. "Monster gone?" Lakshmi whispered. "Just a car going home." Lakshmi counted three more cars before she slept.

qa.q: Where did Lakshmi lie while watching the clouds?
qa.a: On the water tank lid on the terrace, with Amma.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi press her face into Sangeeta's arm?
qa.a: The moving stripes on the ceiling looked like a monster's fingers, and she was scared.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta help Lakshmi, and what made it work?
qa.a: She held her and had her watch the next car make the stripes, so Lakshmi could see the monster was only light.

qa.q: What might Sangeeta be thinking as Lakshmi counts cars?
qa.a: She is probably relieved and glad that Lakshmi's fear has become a small game before sleep.

grounding: A child sees a crocodile cloud with joy and a monster in moving shadows with fear, both from pattern-finding.

passage:
In the kindergarten yard, Tanuja, five, squealed. "A dragon! Look, his tail!" The long cloud curled over the water tank, and she roared at it, laughing.
At nap time the curtains were drawn. On the wall, a dark shape with long arms moved round and round.
"Monster," Tanuja whispered, pulling her blanket up to her nose.
Darshan, the teacher, knelt by her and switched on the small light. The arms were the fan's blades.
"Same trick as your dragon," Darshan said softly. "Your eyes are good at finding shapes."
Tanuja peeped out and waved at the fan.

qa.q: What was really making the moving shape on the wall?
qa.a: The ceiling fan's blades.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling when she pulled her blanket up to her nose?
qa.a: She felt frightened, sure a monster with long arms was moving on the wall.

qa.q: How did Darshan help Tanuja, and why did it work?
qa.a: Darshan switched on a light and showed her the fan, linking it to her dragon, so she could see her own eyes had made the shape.

qa.q: How might Darshan see Tanuja's dragon and monster together?
qa.a: Darshan sees them as the same skill at work, finding shapes, which brings both her joy and her fear.

grounding: It shows a young child delighting in a dragon cloud and fearing a shadow monster, both from finding shapes.

passage:
Saturday. On the terrace, Eshaan, five, pointed at the sky. "Elephant! With a trunk!" He stomped around, trumpeting, and Zeenat Appi laughed.
Sunday night. Eshaan screamed. By the door stood a tall black shape with a big head. "A man," he sobbed. It was Abbu's coat on the hook, lit by the street lamp. Zeenat held him and switched on the lamp. "See? Coat."
Wednesday. Zeenat made a torch rabbit on the wall. Eshaan made a wobbly shape. "Monster!" he said, and this time he laughed.

qa.q: What was the tall black shape by the door?
qa.a: Abbu's coat on the hook, lit by the street lamp.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling when he screamed on Sunday night?
qa.a: He felt terrified, sure a man was standing by the door.

qa.q: What did Zeenat try on Wednesday, and why might it help?
qa.a: She made shadow shapes with him using a torch, so he could see shadows are made by things and enjoy them instead of fearing them.

qa.q: How might Zeenat feel on Sunday night when Eshaan sobs?
qa.a: She might feel worried at first, then gentle and protective as she shows him the coat.

grounding: It shows a young child over several days delighting in a cloud elephant, fearing a coat shadow, then playing with shadows.

passage:
The power went out after dinner. Nitin lit a candle, and the room began to wobble.
All evening Urmila, five, had called out clouds from the balcony. "A running horse!" Now she stared at the wall behind the water jug. A huge dark head with a hooked nose swayed there.
"Papa," she said in a tiny voice. "Monster."
Nitin moved the jug. The head vanished. He put it back. It came again.
Then he held his hands before the flame, and a dog barked silently on the wall.
Urmila giggled. "Now make my horse!"

qa.q: What made the monster head on the wall?
qa.a: The water jug in front of the candle.

qa.q: How did Urmila's voice show what she was feeling?
qa.a: Her tiny voice showed she was scared of the swaying head on the wall.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Urmila, and why?
qa.a: Moving the jug to make the head vanish and come back worked, because she could see the shape came from the jug, and the hand dog turned fear into play.

qa.q: What is it like for Nitin during the power cut?
qa.a: He has to calm his frightened child in a dim room, and he seems patient and playful, using the candle to show how shadows work.

grounding: It shows a young child who delights in a horse cloud and then fears a candle shadow during a power cut.

passage:
In the monsoon, clouds rolled fast over the Mumbai flats. From the balcony Charu squealed, "Mumma, a dragon! See his tail!" Urmila looked; one grey cloud did have a long curly end. Charu roared at it happily.
That night the power went off in the storm, and a car's lights swept across the bedroom wall. The shadow of the clothes stand stretched into a tall, spiky shape. Charu screamed. "A monster!"
Urmila switched on the torch and showed her the clothes stand. "See? The same shape-finding eyes as your dragon." Charu peeked out, still clutching the blanket.

qa.q: What did the clothes stand's shadow look like?
qa.a: A tall, spiky shape.

qa.q: How did Charu feel about the cloud dragon compared with the shadow?
qa.a: The cloud dragon made her delighted and playful, but the shadow made her frightened.

qa.q: What did Urmila do that helped?
qa.a: She shone the torch on the real clothes stand, linking the scary shadow to the same fun shape-finding.

qa.q: How might Urmila feel when Charu screams?
qa.a: She might feel startled and then tender, understanding that the same imagination brings both joy and fear.

grounding: Shows a young child in the monsoon delighting in a cloud dragon and then frightened by a monster shadow, both from the same pattern-finding.

passage:
"Pallavi didi, look at the clouds! A rabbit!"
"Where?"
"There, above the temple. Ears and everything!"
"Oh, yes! And that one's an elephant."
"No, it's a crocodile! Eating the moon!"
That night the Diwali diyas flickered on the wall.
"Didi... there's someone at the window."
"Shankar, it's the diya shadow."
"It's got long fingers. It's moving."
"That's the curtain moving. Look, I'll wave my hand. See? Another shadow."
"...It's the same as my rabbit?"
"Exactly. Your eyes love finding things."
"Can my eyes find a rabbit in this one instead?"
"Try."
"...A rabbit with long fingers."

qa.q: What was the crocodile doing, according to Shankar?
qa.a: Eating the moon!

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling when he saw the shadow on Diwali night?
qa.a: He felt scared, sure someone with long fingers was at the window.

qa.q: How did Pallavi help Shankar with the shadow?
qa.a: She pointed to the moving curtain and made a shadow with her hand, linking it to his cloud game.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel when Shankar finds a rabbit with long fingers?
qa.a: She would likely feel amused and relieved that he turned the fear into play.

grounding: Shows a young child at Diwali finding happy animals in clouds and a frightening figure in diya shadows, both from the same pattern-seeing.

passage:
KG note, winter term. Usha, class teacher.
On our sunny morning walk, Dilnaz spotted a cloud dragon and led the class in roaring at it. She made us wait until its tail blew away.
After lunch, in the darkened room for our shadow-puppet show, the big shadow of my hand-dog made her cry and hide under the table. The same eyes that found the dragon had found a monster. I sat with her, switched on the light and let her make a shadow herself. Soon she was making a baby dragon on the wall.
Tomorrow we'll do shadows with the lights half on.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz spot in the clouds?
qa.a: A dragon.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel during the shadow-puppet show?
qa.a: She felt frightened, crying and hiding under the table at the big shadow.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped Dilnaz?
qa.a: Sat with her, switched on the light, and let her make a shadow herself.

qa.q: How might the other children have felt on the dragon walk?
qa.a: They probably felt excited and joyful, roaring along with Dilnaz.

grounding: A teacher's winter note shows a child delighting in a cloud dragon and frightened by a shadow shape, both coming from the same pattern-finding.

passage: It was the first cool evening after the monsoon in the village near Nashik. Deepak lay on the charpai in the courtyard and pointed. 'Nirmala Didi, a dragon! See his tail!' The cloud did look like a dragon. Deepak roared at it, delighted. Later, inside, the lantern threw the shadow of the hanging sickle on the wall. Deepak froze. 'A monster with a hook hand!' He pulled the sheet over his head. Nirmala moved the lantern. The monster became a sickle again. Deepak peeked out, then giggled. 'It tricked me.'

qa.q: What made the shadow on the wall?
qa.a: The hanging sickle, lit by the lantern.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel when he saw the shadow?
qa.a: Deepak felt frightened, freezing and hiding under the sheet, though a moment later he giggled.

qa.q: What did Nirmala do that helped?
qa.a: She moved the lantern so Deepak could see the monster was only the sickle's shadow.

qa.q: How might Nirmala see Deepak's dragon and monster?
qa.a: She probably finds it sweet and funny that the same imagination makes him both delighted and scared.

grounding: A young child sees a dragon in the clouds with delight and a monster in a shadow with fear, from the same pattern-finding.

passage: In Stockholm in December it was dark by three. Ulla, five, stood at the window with her friend Hiroshi, watching the snow clouds. 'A big bear!' she said. 'With a hat!' They laughed until their breath fogged the glass. At bedtime, the streetlight shone through the bare tree outside, and a shape with long, thin fingers stretched across her ceiling. Ulla screamed for Papa. He sat on the bed and wiggled his own fingers in the light. 'Look, the tree is waving.' Ulla watched, then waved back at it.

qa.q: What did Ulla see in the snow clouds?
qa.a: A big bear with a hat.

qa.q: What did Ulla feel when the shape stretched across her ceiling?
qa.a: Ulla felt scared and screamed, seeing long, thin fingers in the tree's shadow.

qa.q: How did Papa help Ulla, and why did it work?
qa.a: He showed her the shadow came from the tree by wiggling his fingers in the light, which turned the scary shape into something she could wave at.

qa.q: How might Hiroshi have felt at the window?
qa.a: Hiroshi probably felt happy and playful, laughing with Ulla at the cloud bear.

grounding: A young child delights in a bear in the clouds and is frightened by a shadow at night, both from the mind finding shapes.

passage: The hostel of the school for small children in Ooty was quiet during the winter nap time. Irfan lay on his mat and looked at the damp patch on the ceiling. The warden came, sat with him, and hung his jacket over the hooks. 'Where's the man now?' Irfan looked. Just a jacket. He sighed and fell asleep.

grounding: A young child finds an elephant in a damp patch with delight and a man in coat hooks with fear, from the same pattern-finding.

passage:
Saptami afternoon. On the roof, Preeti points at a cloud. "A dragon! With a curly tail!" Bidisha didi squints and laughs. "It's eating the pandal!"
Ashtami night. The pandal lights throw a spiky shadow on the bedroom wall. Preeti pulls the sheet over her head. "Monster," she whispers. Didi holds her hand and flaps the curtain. The monster wobbles and turns back into a curtain.
Navami morning. Preeti makes a shadow bunny on the wall with her own fingers, giggling. "Didi, look! Mine!"

qa.q: What did Preeti see in the cloud on Saptami?
qa.a: A dragon with a curly tail.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel about the spiky shadow on Ashtami night?
qa.a: She felt frightened, pulling the sheet over her head and whispering "Monster", although it was only the pandal lights on the curtain.

qa.q: What helped Preeti with the shadow, and why?
qa.a: Bidisha didi held her hand and flapped the curtain so the monster wobbled back into a curtain, letting Preeti see where the shape came from.

qa.q: What would change if Bidisha had said "Don't be silly, go to sleep"?
qa.a: Preeti might have stayed scared of the wall in the dark, and might not have found out on Navami that she could make shadow shapes herself.

grounding: A child finds a dragon in a cloud and a monster in a night shadow, delight and fear coming from the same shape-finding.
